prompt: In the planner's course screen, the list ticks the sessions done and the footer adds them up. Where should `done` live?
hint: One fact, one owner.

choices.text: In the row, and the footer asks each row
choices.why: Then the row is an owner and the footer depends on rows being on screen; the fact belongs in the plan.

choices.text: Once, in the plan the screen draws from
choices.why: Right. The list and the total are both computed from it, so they cannot disagree.

choices.text: In both the list and the footer, kept in step after each tap
choices.why: Two copies kept in step is exactly what goes wrong the first time a step is forgotten.

choices.text: In the `Toggle`, which remembers whether it is on
choices.why: A `Toggle` keeps nothing: it is handed a binding to somebody else's `Bool`.

prompt: Which of these is a second source of truth waiting to disagree?
hint: Can it be computed from the plan?

choices.text: The plan's list of sessions
choices.why: That is the source of truth itself.

choices.text: A `Binding` to the plan, handed to the detail screen
choices.why: A binding holds no value; it reads and writes the owner's.

choices.text: A `total` property set once from `weekTotal`
choices.why: Right: it can be computed, so storing it makes a copy that goes stale.

choices.text: The course's `id`, which never changes
choices.why: It is part of the data, not derived from it.

prompt: Why can a SwiftUI view not keep a counter in an ordinary `var` property?
hint: What happens to the struct when the parent's body runs?

choices.text: The struct is made again, and the new copy starts from the initial value
choices.why: Right. `@State` keeps the value outside the struct for that reason.

choices.text: Structs cannot have `var` properties
choices.why: They can; lesson 1's `Plan` has two.

choices.text: SwiftUI makes every property `let` at compile time
choices.why: Nothing rewrites your properties; `body` is not `mutating`, and the struct is replaced.

choices.text: A `var` is shared between every copy of the view
choices.why: Each copy of a struct has its own properties; that is the problem, not the cure.

prompt: A parent creates `CourseDetailView(plan: newPlan)` with a different plan while the view is on screen. The view stores it with `_plan = State(initialValue: plan)`. What does it show?
hint: When does SwiftUI use the initial value?

choices.text: The new plan, because the initialiser ran again
choices.why: It ran, and SwiftUI ignored the value: the storage it kept wins.

choices.text: The old plan, from the storage SwiftUI kept
choices.why: Right. The initial value is used the first time the view appears and not after.

choices.text: An empty plan, because the two values conflict
choices.why: There is no merging; one value is kept.

choices.text: A runtime error saying state was set twice
choices.why: Nothing complains, which is why this trap is hard to see.

prompt: Why does Apple's documentation say to declare `@State` properties `private`?
hint: Who owns the value?

choices.text: Private properties are faster to read
choices.why: Access control is about who may see a name, not speed.

choices.text: SwiftUI refuses to compile public state
choices.why: It compiles; the advice is about design.

choices.text: The view owns it, and nothing outside should set it
choices.why: Right. A parent that wants to influence it passes a starting value or owns the state itself.

choices.text: So that a binding to it cannot be made with `$`
choices.why: `$plan` works inside the view, and that binding is exactly what children receive.

prompt: Inside the initialiser, `_plan` names the property ___ itself, not the plan inside it.
hint: Two words in the lesson; the blank is the second.

prompt: What does a `Binding<Bool>` handed to a `Toggle` contain?
hint: Not the value.

choices.text: A copy of the `Bool` taken when the toggle was made
choices.why: A copy would fall behind; a binding reaches the owner's value.

choices.text: A way to read the value and a way to write it
choices.why: Right: two operations that reach back to wherever the owner keeps it.

choices.text: The view that owns the value
choices.why: It does not know the owner; the value could be in `@State` or an object.

choices.text: A notification name to post on change
choices.why: No notifications are involved; the write goes straight to the storage.

prompt: In `ForEach($plan.sessions) { $session in … }`, what is `session` inside the closure?
hint: The closure's parameter is declared with a dollar sign.

choices.text: Another binding, the same as `$session`
choices.why: `$session` is the binding; without the sign it is the value.

choices.text: The index of the session in the array
choices.why: `ForEach` over a collection of `Identifiable` values gives elements, not indices.

choices.text: The session's current value
choices.why: Right; `$session` is the binding to it, and reading `session` reads through it.

choices.text: A private copy the row can change freely, saved when the row disappears
choices.why: There is no private copy and no saving later; writes go through at once.

prompt: A preview wants to show `SessionRow` with no parent. Which binding does it pass?
hint: One that ignores writes.

choices.text: `$session`, from a `let` in the preview
choices.why: A `let` has no projected value; `$` works on `@State` and `@Binding`.

choices.text: `.constant(…)`, a binding that ignores writes
choices.why: Right. `Binding.constant` is the standard way to give a view a fixed value.

choices.text: `nil`, since bindings are optional
choices.why: `@Binding var session: StudySession` is not optional.

choices.text: A new `@State`, declared at the top of the file
choices.why: `@State` belongs inside a view, not at the top level of a file.

prompt: Match each piece of syntax to what it is.
hint: The dollar sign is the projected value.

pairs.right: A binding to the whole plan
A binding narrowed to one field

right_distractors: A copy of the plan for the child

prompt: `binding.swift` printed `a copy:` first. How many sessions were done in the storage at that point?
hint: Read the list after `storage is`.

prompt: In `Ref`, why is the setter of `value` declared `nonmutating`?
hint: What does setting `value` change?

choices.text: So that `Ref` can be a class
choices.why: It is a struct; `nonmutating` exists for structs.

choices.text: Because key paths only work on immutable values
choices.why: The subscript takes a `WritableKeyPath`, which is for writing.

choices.text: Setting it calls `write` and leaves the `Ref` itself unchanged
choices.why: Right, so a `let` holding a `Ref`, like `DoneToggle.isOn`, can still be written through.

choices.text: So the compiler copies the storage on every write
choices.why: Nothing is copied; the closure writes into the `Storage` box.

prompt: `sessions[1].done` compiles although `Ref` declares no `subscript(Int)`. What makes it work?
hint: Look at the attribute on the type.

choices.text: Swift adds an integer subscript to every generic struct
choices.why: It adds nothing of the kind; something in `Ref` asked for it.

choices.text: `@dynamicMemberLookup` turns `[1]` and `.done` into key paths for the subscript
choices.why: Right: Swift builds `\.[1]` and `\.done` and calls `subscript(dynamicMember:)` with each.

choices.text: `Storage` is a class, so its contents are reachable by index
choices.why: The expression is on `sessions`, a `Ref`, not on the storage.

choices.text: `print` converts the expression at run time
choices.why: It is resolved when compiling; `print` only receives the result.

prompt: Put the three lines `binding.swift` printed in the order they appeared.
hint: Copy, binding, narrowed.

prompt: The failing test expected 150. What did `screen.total.done` actually hold?
hint: Swift Testing printed the left-hand side.

prompt: Why does `DerivedTotal` pass where `StoredTotal` fails?
hint: When is each total worked out?

choices.text: `DerivedTotal` uses a different `weekTotal`
choices.why: Both call lesson 1's `weekTotal(today:)`.

choices.text: `StoredTotal` marks a different session done
choices.why: Both tests mark `s3`.

choices.text: Swift Testing runs computed properties before stored ones
choices.why: Test order has nothing to do with it; each test has its own value.

choices.text: Its total is computed when read, after the change
choices.why: Right. The stored one was computed in `init` and never told about `s3`.

prompt: A colleague keeps `StoredTotal` and adds a line updating `total` after every `markDone`. What is still wrong?
hint: How many ways are there to change a plan?

choices.text: Every other change, `add` included, needs the same line, and one will be missed
choices.why: Right: the copy stays correct only while every writer remembers it.

choices.text: Nothing; the test passes now, so the design is sound
choices.why: It passes for `markDone`; the next kind of change brings the bug back.

choices.text: `total` cannot be assigned because it is a `let`
choices.why: It is a `var` in `StoredTotal`.

choices.text: `weekTotal` is too slow to call that often
choices.why: It filters a short list; speed is not the problem here.

prompt: A `SessionForm` keeps `@State private var draft = Draft()`, where `Draft` is a class. The stepper changes `draft.minutes` and the number on screen stays put. Why?
hint: What does `@State` watch?

choices.text: Steppers only work with `Int` state, not properties
choices.why: A stepper works with any `Binding` to a strideable value.

choices.text: The reference did not change, so `@State` saw nothing
choices.why: Right. Make `Draft` a struct, or make it observable as lesson 7 does.

choices.text: `Draft()` is created again on every update and starts at 30
choices.why: The initial value is used once; the same object is kept.

choices.text: Classes cannot be stored in a property wrapper at all
choices.why: They can be stored; changes inside them are not seen.

prompt: A parent and its child each declare `@State var plan`, the child's initialised from the parent's. The child adds a session. What does the parent show?
hint: Count the owners.

choices.text: The new session, since the child's plan came from the parent
choices.why: It came from the parent once; after that there are two plans.

choices.text: A crash, since two states hold one plan
choices.why: Nothing crashes; they hold two plans.

choices.text: The old plan: there are two plans, and only the child's changed
choices.why: Right. The child should take a `@Binding` to the parent's plan.

choices.text: The new session, after the parent's body runs again
choices.why: The parent's state did not change, so its body has nothing new to draw.

prompt: Which of these is a good use of `@State` in the planner?
hint: Something that starts with the view and nobody else needs.

choices.text: The plan in `CourseDetailView`, copied from the list
choices.why: That makes a second owner; the detail screen takes a binding.

choices.text: Whether the week screen's breakdown is expanded
choices.why: Right: it belongs to that view, starts with it and matters to nobody else.

choices.text: The week's total, kept up to date by each row
choices.why: It can be computed, so it should be.

choices.text: The list of courses every screen shows
choices.why: Shared by several screens, so it belongs above them, as lesson 7 does.

prompt: In section 08, why does `CourseDetailView` take `@Binding var plan` instead of `@State`?
hint: Who owns the plan?

choices.text: `@State` is not allowed in a view opened by a `NavigationLink`
choices.why: It is allowed; it would just be a second owner here.

choices.text: The list owns it, and the detail screen changes it
choices.why: Right: a change made on the detail screen has to land in the list's one plan.

choices.text: Bindings are faster to draw than state
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; ownership is.

choices.text: A binding lets the detail screen keep its own copy of the plan
choices.why: A binding is the opposite of a copy.

prompt: Put the steps of one tap on a `SessionRow` toggle in order.
hint: From the finger to the footer.
items: SwiftUI runs `body` again for the views that read it
The footer computes `weekTotal` from the new plan

prompt: Which of these hold no value of their own? Choose all that apply.
hint: A binding reaches somebody else's.

choices.text: `@Binding var session: StudySession`
choices.why: Yes: it reads and writes the owner's session.

choices.text: `@State private var plan: Plan`
choices.why: No: this is the owner, and SwiftUI keeps the value for it.

choices.text: The `Ref` built in section 05
choices.why: Yes: two closures, and the value is in `Storage`.

choices.text: `let plan: Plan` passed to read
choices.why: No: a `let` holds a copy, the read-only one.
